HELM VALUES SCHEMA CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does your values.yaml actually match its own schema?

Paste a Helm chart's values.yaml and its values.schema.json and get a deterministic report: every field values.yaml sets that the schema never declares -- the exact shape a typo like imgae: instead of image: takes, and helm lint misses unless the schema forbids extra fields outright -- plus every real schema violation (missing required field, wrong type, bad enum value, out-of-range number).

Nothing is uploaded. Files you load are read in this browser and never leave your device. No Helm binary, no cluster, no network call.

1. Load your files

2. What Helm would silently accept, and what it would reject

FieldSeverityFinding

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same checker, zero dependencies, two files — run it against a chart repo before every release, no Helm install required:

node cli.mjs check chart/values.yaml chart/values.schema.json               # exit 1 on any real schema violation
node cli.mjs check chart/values.yaml chart/values.schema.json --strict      # also fail on undeclared fields
node cli.mjs check chart/values.yaml chart/values.schema.json --json

Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the local files you name: no network call, ever.

What this checks — and what it cannot

It understands the JSON Schema subset that covers the overwhelming majority of real charts: type, properties, required, additionalProperties, enum, minimum/maximum, and items for arrays. See why this class of typo happens for how Helm's template engine actually behaves on an undefined key.

Already have Helm installed? See how this differs from helm lint — short version: same schema, but this also flags the undeclared-field case most schemas leave unguarded. A schema that matches values.yaml perfectly still says nothing about whether the chart's templates render correctly — this checks the data against its own contract, not the rendered manifests. Once you have rendered the chart, see Kubernetes Deprecated API Check for whether the output uses an apiVersion your target cluster will reject outright.

Prefer to just read the two files side by side? See what a manual read catches, and what gets hard as the schema grows nested fields.

Common questions

Doesn't helm lint already catch this?

Only partly. helm lint applies values.schema.json if the chart ships one, but most schemas leave additionalProperties unset (JSON Schema's permissive default), so an undeclared field — the exact shape a typo like imgae instead of image takes — passes lint silently. This tool flags that case too, as informational rather than a hard failure, because it is very often exactly the mistake it looks like.

Do I need Helm installed to use this?

No. It reads plain YAML and JSON text with its own parser — no Helm binary, no chart dependency resolution, no cluster, no network call, in the browser or the CLI.

Is my values.yaml uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses a pasted or locally loaded file entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only local files — no network call, ever.

What JSON Schema features does it understand?

type, properties, required, additionalProperties, enum, minimum, maximum, and items for arrays — the subset that covers the overwhelming majority of real Helm values.schema.json files. It does not evaluate $ref, oneOf/anyOf/allOf, or regex patterns; a schema using those is read but those specific rules are not checked.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not infrastructure, security, or compliance advice, and it does not replace testing an actual helm install --dry-run against a real cluster. It checks the JSON Schema subset it supports against the values you supplied — it cannot prove your chart renders correctly, only report the mismatches it found. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. Files you load are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded, file_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checking-it-by-eye.html.text:
← Back to Helm Values Schema Check

This checker vs. eyeballing values.yaml against the schema

A careful reader genuinely catches the obvious case: a top-level field with a type that's clearly wrong, a required field that's visibly missing on a short file. This page names no company or product — reading values.yaml next to values.schema.json before a release is a habit most chart authors already have, not a competing tool.

What a side-by-side read catches reliably

The mismatches that sit in plain sight on a short chart are the ones a reader who knows the schema already catches well: replicaCount: "three" where the schema says integer, or a whole required block left out entirely. This tool's type-mismatch and missing-required checks flag exactly the same fields, for the same reason.

What gets harder as the schema grows nested objects and lists

CaseReading by eyeThis tool
A typo'd nested key, e.g. image.repositryDepends on holding the schema's full property tree in mind while scanning every line of values.yaml — a field that's merely unused looks identical to one that's misspelledWalks every declared path in the schema against every field values.yaml actually sets, at any depth, every time
An enum value that's close but wrong, e.g. pullPolicy: IfNotPresntReads as plausible unless the reader happens to recall the schema's exact allowed list for that fieldenum-violation checks the literal value against the schema's declared list
A number outside its minimum/maximum, e.g. replicaCount: 0 against minimum: 1Looks like an ordinary integer unless the reader checked that field's bound a moment beforebelow-minimum/above-maximum compare every numeric field against its declared bound
Several unrelated mismatches scattered through a long fileEach individually findable; keeping a running tally of all of them while reading top to bottom is where a manual pass degradesReports every finding in one pass, in the same order, regardless of file length

The gap that matters most: cross-referencing every field, not skimming for one

Whether a nested field is declared, whether an enum value is one of the allowed strings, and whether a number sits inside its bound are none of them visible on the line itself — each depends on a separate part of the schema the reader has to keep in mind while scanning a completely different part of values.yaml. That cross-referencing is the part that degrades fastest as a chart's schema grows more nested objects and lists. This tool walks the same schema tree against the same values on every run, regardless of how deep or how long either file is.

When to still read the files yourself

This is a schema check, not a chart renderer — it has no connection to Helm's templates, so a values.yaml that matches its schema perfectly can still produce a broken manifest, and this tool would not know. It also evaluates only the JSON Schema subset listed on the checker itself — $ref, oneOf/anyOf/allOf, and regex patterns are read but not enforced. Deciding whether a flagged field actually matters for your deployment, and checking schema rules this tool doesn't evaluate, is still a job for reading the files yourself.

Common questions

What does reading values.yaml against the schema by eye actually catch?

A reader who knows the chart catches the obvious case reliably: a top-level field with a type that's clearly wrong, or a required field that's visibly absent on a short file. Those are real mismatches and a careful side-by-side read finds them the same way this tool's type-mismatch and missing-required checks do.

Why is a typo'd nested field hard to catch by eye?

Whether image.repositry is a typo of image.repository depends on knowing every key the schema declares under image, at whatever nesting depth it sits — not a property visible on the line itself. On a chart with a shallow schema this is manageable; on one with several nested objects the reader has to hold the schema's whole property tree in mind while scanning every line of values.yaml, and a field that is merely unused rather than misspelled looks identical to one that is.

Why is an enum or min/max violation easy to miss when reading by hand?

The schema states the allowed enum values or numeric bounds once, often far from any given use of the field, so catching a violation means remembering that list or range while reading a completely different part of the file. A pullPolicy of IfNotPresnt reads as plausible unless the reader happens to recall the exact three strings Kubernetes accepts; a replicaCount of 0 against a minimum of 1 looks like an ordinary integer unless the reader checked the schema's minimum for that exact field a moment before.

Does a long values.yaml make this worse?

Yes, and not in proportion to its length — a reviewer has to hold the schema's structure in mind for every field, and the chance of missing one violation among dozens of nested keys rises with each additional field, not staying flat the way a short, hand-checkable file does. This tool checks every field against the schema the same way regardless of how many there are.

Does this replace understanding what a flagged field does?

No. This is a schema check, not a chart renderer — it has no connection to Helm's templates, so it cannot tell you whether a value that matches the schema will actually produce a working manifest. Deciding whether a flagged field matters for your deployment, and reading schema features this tool doesn't evaluate ($ref, oneOf/anyOf/allOf, regex patterns), is still a job for reading the files yourself.

Check values.yaml against its schema

No warranty. This page and the linked tool are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not infrastructure or compliance advice, and it does not replace testing an actual helm install --dry-run against a real cluster. You are responsible for verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

vs-helm-lint.html.text:
← Back to Helm Values Schema Check

This checker vs. helm lint

helm lint is Helm's own built-in validator. It checks chart structure, required metadata, template syntax, and -- since Helm 3.5 -- a chart's values.yaml against its values.schema.json, if the chart ships one. It needs the Helm binary installed and, for full coverage, a chart directory it can actually render.

This checker validates only one relationship -- values.yaml against values.schema.json -- with no Helm install required, and closes one specific gap: most real schemas leave additionalProperties unset, so a field values.yaml sets that the schema never mentions is not a schema violation and helm lint says nothing about it. This checker flags it anyway, as informational, because that is very often exactly what a typo looks like.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Check chart structure, required metadata (Chart.yaml), and template syntax. helm lint -- this checker does not read templates at all.
Render templates and check the actual output against a live or simulated cluster. helm template / helm install --dry-run -- this checker never renders anything.
Enforce a schema that already sets additionalProperties: false. Either -- both reject an undeclared field the same way once the schema forbids it.
Catch a typo'd values.yaml key when the schema does not set additionalProperties: false (most charts). This checker -- helm lint is silent here by design, since JSON Schema treats an undeclared field as allowed unless told otherwise.
Validate values.yaml against a schema with no Helm binary installed at all -- a script, a pre-commit hook, a CI job that should not depend on it. This checker -- node cli.mjs check values.yaml values.schema.json, nothing to install.
Get a pass/fail on the values/schema relationship alone, separate from template or chart-metadata errors muddying the result. This checker -- it only ever reports on values.yaml vs. values.schema.json.

These compose rather than compete. Keep helm lint (and helm template) as the tool of record for chart structure and rendering -- this checker does not touch either. Add this checker where you specifically want the undeclared-field case caught without depending on a schema author having remembered additionalProperties: false, or where the Helm binary is not available at all (a lightweight CI job, a pre-commit hook, a script bundled with a values-file generator).

Common questions

Should I use this checker or helm lint?

Use both — they overlap but are not the same check. helm lint validates chart structure and templates, and applies values.schema.json if the chart has one and Helm is installed. This checker validates only values.yaml against values.schema.json, with no Helm install required, and — the specific gap — flags a field values.yaml sets that the schema never mentions even when additionalProperties is not set to false, which is the common case and the one a typo actually produces. helm lint stays the tool of record for template rendering, chart metadata, and anything this checker does not claim to cover.

Doesn't helm lint already apply values.schema.json?

Yes, if the chart has one — Helm has supported values.schema.json validation since 3.5. What it enforces depends on the schema's own additionalProperties setting: with additionalProperties: false, an undeclared field is rejected exactly the way this checker's "high severity" finding reports it. Without that setting — the JSON Schema default, and what most real charts actually ship — an undeclared field is not a schema violation, so helm lint says nothing about it. This checker flags it anyway, as an informational finding, because in practice it is very often a typo rather than an intentional omission.

Why would I use this instead of just running helm lint?

Two reasons. First, no Helm install: this is one dependency-free JavaScript file plus a browser page, useful in a script or CI job that should not depend on the Helm binary being present. Second, the undeclared-field gap above — if your chart's schema does not set additionalProperties: false (most don't), helm lint will not tell you about a typo'd values.yaml key, and this checker will. It does not replace helm lint's template rendering and chart-metadata checks; it is narrower and catches one specific thing more of the time.

Is this page affiliated with the Helm project or the CNCF?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the Helm project, the CNCF, or the Helm maintainers. Helm is named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, and to compare against helm lint's own values.schema.json support, described on Helm's own documentation site.

Only point either tool at a chart you own or are authorised to test. That rule is unchanged by which one you pick.

← Back to the checker

No warranty. This is not infrastructure or compliance advice. It checks the JSON Schema subset it supports against the values you supplied -- it cannot prove your chart renders correctly, only report the mismatches it found. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

Everything on the checker runs client-side; nothing is uploaded. Support is optional and never changes what the tool does.

why-helm-silently-accepts-a-typo-in-valu.text:
← Back to Helm Values Schema Check

Why Helm silently accepts a typo in values.yaml

The mechanism

A Helm chart template reads values.yaml through Go's text/template/html/template engine as .Values.image.repository, a lookup into a plain nested map. Go's template engine returns the zero value for a map key that was never set -- an empty string, not an error. So if values.yaml actually sets image.repositry (missing an "o"), the template asking for .Values.image.repository gets back nothing, the typo'd key sits there unused, and the chart renders successfully -- usually with a blank, or a hard-coded chart default silently standing in for what the user meant to override.

Nothing about the render signals this went wrong. helm template exits 0. The Pod comes up, possibly pulling the chart's default image instead of the one the values file was supposed to specify, and the mistake surfaces later, if at all -- as a "why is it running the wrong version" investigation days after the values file was written and reviewed.

Why helm lint does not catch it

Helm has supported values.schema.json validation since 3.5.0 -- a real, useful gate, when a chart ships one. But JSON Schema's default for an object is permissive: a field the schema does not mention in properties is allowed unless the schema explicitly sets additionalProperties: false on that object. Most real charts' schemas -- written once, rarely revisited -- do not set it. So image.repositry next to a schema that declares image.repository is, as far as JSON Schema and therefore helm lint are concerned, just an extra field. Not required, not forbidden, not wrong. Lint passes. The typo ships.

Schema saysvalues.yaml sets image.repositry (typo)helm lint result
additionalProperties: falseRejectedFails -- the schema is doing its job
unset (JSON Schema default)Allowed as an extra fieldPasses -- lint has nothing to object to

What this tool looks for, and why it stops where it does

It walks values.yaml against values.schema.json and reports two different things at two different severities. A real schema violation -- a missing required field, a wrong type, a value outside an enum or a minimum/maximum, or a field forbidden by an explicit additionalProperties: false -- is reported as something helm install --dry-run --validate would already reject. A field the schema simply does not mention is reported too, but as informational: it is not a schema violation, but it is very often exactly the mistake it looks like, and the alternative -- staying silent the way helm lint does -- is how the typo ships.

It reads plain YAML and JSON text with its own parser -- no Helm binary, no chart dependency resolution (Chart.yaml's dependencies are not walked), no cluster, no network call. That is what makes it safe to run against a chart repository with nothing installed and no credentials granted at all.

What this is not

This is not a replacement for helm lint or helm template -- it does not read chart templates, Chart.yaml metadata, or subchart dependency resolution at all, and a values file that matches its schema perfectly can still render a broken chart for reasons entirely outside values.yaml. It is also not a full JSON Schema implementation: it understands type, properties, required, additionalProperties, enum, minimum/maximum, and items, not $ref, oneOf/anyOf/allOf, or regex pattern. See how this differs from helm lint for exactly where each tool's coverage stops.

Common questions

What actually happens when a chart template reads a values.yaml key that isn't set?

Go's text/template and html/template packages, which Helm renders through, return the zero value for a missing map key rather than an error -- an empty string for .Values.image.repository if it was never set. The template renders successfully with a blank or a chart default standing in for whatever the typo'd key should have provided, and nothing about the render itself signals that anything went wrong.

Why doesn't helm lint catch this?

helm lint validates values.yaml against values.schema.json only if the chart ships one, and even then only enforces additionalProperties: false if the schema author set it -- JSON Schema's default is to allow fields it does not mention. Most real charts' schemas do not set it, so a field values.yaml sets that the schema never declares -- exactly the shape a typo takes -- is not a schema violation at all, and lint says nothing about it.

Does the required: true option in values.schema.json help?

It helps with a different half of the same problem. required catches a key the schema expects that values.yaml never sets at all. It does not catch the reverse: a key values.yaml does set, under a name the schema does not recognize, sitting right next to the correctly-named one it was supposed to override. Both are worth checking, and this tool checks both.

No warranty. This is not infrastructure or compliance advice. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

Everything here runs client-side; nothing is uploaded. Support is optional and never changes what the tool does.
